newsitem.title: INDIA: India politicians invoked to help end truck strike.
newsitem.headline: India politicians invoked to help end truck strike.

text.p: India's striking truck owners kept more than two million vehicles off the road for a seventh day on Monday after seeking guidance from political parties on how to break the deadlock, transport officials said.
"We had meetings with government officials and leaders of political parties on Sunday," S.P. Singh, spokesman for the All India Motor Transport Congress (AIMTC), told Reuters.
"We are open to negotiations."
But he said the strike would continue as long as a proposed service tax was still on the cards.
The AIMTC is opposed to the five percent service tax on road transport that Finance Minister P. Chidambaram proposed in the federal budget for financial 1997/98 (April-March).
It is also protesting a sharp rise in insurance premiums.
"The issue of insurance is likely to be resolved earlier than the service tax," Singh said.
"Until our demands are met we will continue the strike."
AIMTC had met parliament's finance panel to discuss their demands, he said.
Small transporters who own one or two trucks constitute 93 percent of the country's total fleet.
The politicians were hopeful a solution could be found soon, Singh said. The truck owners launched their strike on April 1.

The government has offered to refer the rise in insurance premiums to the tariff advisory committee. "We have told the tariff advisory committee we will hold discussions with them," a senior government official told Reuters.
Economists and industry leaders said the strike was hitting the economy hard, paralysing trade, pushing up prices and affecting the livelihood of daily wage earners.
The peaceful protest has kept 2.2 million trucks off the road since it began.

"If the strike continues, it will have alarming repercussions leading to an acute shortage of essential commodities and a significant push to prices...," A.S. Kasliwal, president of the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry, said in a statement.

"Movement of essential commodities has suffered, prices of foodgrains have gone up by nearly 25 percent, export shipments have been affected as goods are not reaching the ports and small units have been closed down," said economist Kulbir Singh of the independent Institute of Economic Sudies.
India was losing 10 billion rupees ($280 million) each day, he said.
AIMTC said its representatives would meet government officials later on Monday.
The government has said that since parliament is still considering the budget, it is for lawmakers to decide whether to drop the proposed service tax.
Singh estimated the cost of the strike to truck owners at nearly four billion rupees ($110 million) a day. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
